item.title: NZD firms in early Asia as New Zealand faces weeks of political limbo
item.description:
The kiwi’s early gain looks more like a thin-liquidity Monday open than a verdict on the election. The result won’t be settled until the final count on November 27, and coalition talks could run for weeks after that. A prolonged hung outcome would keep a layer of political risk on the currency. The loss of Finance Minister Nicola Willis’s seat adds uncertainty over fiscal direction in a second term. Until the count firms up, global risk sentiment, US dollar moves and RBNZ expectations are likely to matter more for NZD/USD than the election itself.

---

Earlier today so far:

  • Suspected Iranian drone strike halts Iraq gas field, cuts two thirds of Kurdistan power
  • Weekend: Trump says new Iran strikes ‘highly unlikely’ five times (but three carriers stay ready)
  • Three risks for Nvidia shares after Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy
  • WTI oil price outlook: After a 17.5% slide, can buyers reclaim $92.53?
  • Gold analysis: Buyers keep defending $4,040. Is $4,140 the next target?

---

The kiwi opened the week firmer, but with Luxon’s coalition clinging to a wafer-thin majority and 400,000 votes still uncounted, New Zealand’s election has produced a wait-and-see market rather than a verdict.

Summary:

  • NZD/USD rose around 0.5% in very early Asian trade on Monday, the first session since Saturday’s election.
  • Preliminary results give the National-led coalition 67 of 131 seats, against a projected 57 for the Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori bloc.
  • Nearly 400,000 special votes are yet to be counted. Final results are due November 27, and coalition talks could take weeks after that.
  • National’s vote share fell to around 29% from about 38% in 2023, while ACT and New Zealand First gained ground.
  • Finance Minister Nicola Willis was among the senior National lawmakers who lost their seats.
  • The centrist Opportunity Party won nearly 6% and could become kingmaker if the coalition falls short.

The New Zealand dollar edged around 0.5% higher against the US dollar in very early Asian trade on Monday. It was the first session since a knife-edge general election that has left the country facing weeks of political uncertainty.

Preliminary results from Saturday’s vote give Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National-led coalition a paper-thin majority, with 67 seats in an expanded 131-seat parliament. The margin is so narrow that a small shift in the final count could still open a path to power for the left-leaning opposition bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, which is projected to hold 57 seats. Nearly 400,000 special votes, including those cast by New Zealanders overseas, are yet to be counted.

Luxon told supporters in Auckland that his party appeared to have a pathway to government but that the race was too close to call. Final official results from the Electoral Commission are due on November 27, and coalition negotiations could take weeks after that. Labour leader Chris Hipkins did not concede, insisting that every vote must be counted.

The result points to deep voter frustration over fuel prices and other living costs, stubbornly high unemployment and healthcare. The government’s economic agenda has been complicated by US tariff uncertainty and the surge in fuel prices driven by the war with Iran. National’s share of the vote fell to around 29% from about 38% in 2023. Its partners ACT and New Zealand First lifted their shares to roughly 11% and 10%, strengthening their hand in any coalition talks and raising the prospect of a government that tilts further to the right.

For markets, one notable casualty is Finance Minister Nicola Willis, who lost her seat along with several other senior National lawmakers. That leaves questions over who would steer fiscal policy in a second term.

The centrist Opportunity Party, led by political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is projected to enter parliament with nearly 6% of the vote, the first outsider party to do so in three decades. Luxon had ruled out working with the party before the election, but he struck a more conciliatory tone on Sunday. Should the coalition fall short once special votes are counted, Opportunity could find itself as kingmaker, courted by both blocs.

Until the final count, the election outcome is likely to remain a background source of uncertainty for the kiwi rather than a clear directional driver.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Suspected Iranian drone strike halts Iraq gas field, cuts two thirds of Kurdistan power
item.description:
The direct supply hit is regional. Khor Mor’s gas feeds Kurdistan’s power plants rather than export markets, so crude and LNG balances are largely untouched. The bigger signal for oil is that energy infrastructure in the region is still being targeted while diplomacy is supposedly picking up. That supports the war-risk premium in crude and undercuts the de-escalation tone in Trump’s latest remarks. Traders will be watching for any confirmed Iranian link, or a US response, that could revive escalation risk around Gulf supply routes.

---

Earlier:

  • Weekend: Trump says new Iran strikes ‘highly unlikely’ five times (but three carriers stay ready)

---

Hours after Trump said renewed US strikes on Iran were unlikely, a suspected Iranian drone knocked out most of Kurdistan’s power supply, a reminder that the region’s energy infrastructure remains a live target whatever the diplomatic mood.

Summary:

  • A drone strike on Sunday evening hit a gas storage facility at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, halting production.
  • The Kurdistan region lost nearly 2.8 gigawatts of generation, roughly two thirds of its normal power supply.
  • No group has claimed responsibility. Iran or its allied Iraqi militias are suspected.
  • The attack came hours after Trump said renewed US military action against Iran was highly unlikely if talks progress.
  • The field supplies regional power generation rather than exports, so the direct global supply impact is limited.
  • Washington is separately pressing Iraq to close all but two border crossings with Iran.

A suspected Iranian drone strike has halted production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, one of the largest in the Kurdistan region. It knocked out nearly 2.8 gigawatts of power generation in what appears to be a significant escalation in the regional fallout from the Iran war.

Two security sources told Reuters that a drone targeted the field on Sunday evening, with smoke seen rising from the site in Chamchamal, Sulaymaniyah province. An engineer at the field said a gas storage facility was hit, and all crew were ordered into shelters for fear of further attacks.

The Kurdistan region’s electricity ministry said nearly 2.8 gigawatts of generating capacity was lost from the grid. With the region normally producing around 4 gigawatts, that implies roughly two thirds of its power supply was taken offline, leaving households and businesses facing outages.

No group has claimed responsibility. Suspicion has fallen on Iran or its allied militias in Iraq, which have carried out repeated missile and drone attacks on the Kurdistan region since the war began. Kurdish authorities have long blamed Iran-backed armed groups for strikes on Khor Mor. The field has been hit many times in recent years, including an attack in November last year that also halted production.

The timing stands out. The strike came only hours after US President Donald Trump said renewed US military action against Iran was highly unlikely as long as talks over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the Strait of Hormuz made progress. If Iranian involvement is confirmed, the attack would suggest that Tehran or its proxies are still prepared to hit regional energy infrastructure even as diplomatic contacts pick up.

Khor Mor is operated by Pearl Petroleum, a consortium that includes UAE-based Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum. Its gas feeds power plants in the Kurdistan region rather than export markets, so the direct effect on global supply is limited.

Pressure on Iraq is also building from Washington. Iraq’s foreign minister said the US Treasury has asked Baghdad to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran, as part of a wider push to tighten economic pressure on Tehran.

Attention now turns to how quickly production can be restored, whether responsibility is formally assigned, and how Washington responds to an attack that cuts across its message of restraint. 

----

In other news, this is expected to have an impact on tech:

  • Three risks for Nvidia shares after Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend: Trump says new Iran strikes ‘highly unlikely’ five times (but three carriers stay ready)
item.description:
For oil, Trump’s comments trim the risk that the US resumes strikes, which could take some of the war-risk premium out of crude. Physical supply risk hasn’t changed, though: Hormuz remains contested and tankers are still being attacked, so any relief is likely to be limited until talks produce something concrete. The tail risk also cuts both ways. With three carriers in place and targets already identified, a breakdown in talks could quickly put escalation back in the price. Any easing in crude would also take a little pressure off the inflation argument behind Fed hike expectations, but that depends on the talks actually moving.

---

Unrelated, but the big news for tech heading into this new week:

  • Three risks for Nvidia shares after Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy

---

Trump is signalling that he would rather settle than strike, but with carriers in position, sanctions tightening and Hormuz still contested, the burden is on Tehran to deliver progress before the military option comes back into play.

Summary:

  • Trump said renewed US military action against Iran is “highly unlikely” as long as talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme and reopening the Strait of Hormuz make progress.
  • He said three US aircraft carriers are in the region and that infrastructure targets, including power plants and bridges, have been identified, though he would prefer not to hit them.
  • Trump claimed Iran’s air defences are destroyed and that it retains only about 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capability.
  • The war is in an eight-month stalemate, with Iranian attacks on tankers in Hormuz and little visible diplomatic progress.
  • Washington is adding pressure: a reward of up to $20 million for nuclear programme information and a task force to block land transfers of weapons.
  • Diplomatic contacts have increased since the US midterms, including a Trump call with Qatar’s emir on de-escalation.

US President Donald Trump has said it is “highly unlikely” he will need to order renewed military action against Iran, provided negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz show progress. He repeated the point five times during a roughly 20-minute phone interview with CNN on Sunday.

Trump tied the outcome to whether Iran signs what he called a very strong agreement, while stressing that he would act if necessary. He argued that Tehran is under severe economic strain, claiming its inflation rate had reached around 300% this year, and said US strikes had already hit the country hard. In his view, Iran is keen to reach a deal.

He also made clear that US forces remain in position. Trump said three aircraft carriers are now in the region, with the latest having just arrived. He said the US has identified infrastructure targets, including power plants and dozens of bridges that he said could be brought down within an hour. He added that he would prefer not to destroy that infrastructure, given how long it would take to rebuild.

On Iran’s defensive capacity, Trump claimed its air defences had been destroyed. He also claimed the regime retains only around 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capability, as many of its factories have been knocked out. These figures have not been independently verified.

Eight months into the war, the two sides have been locked in a stalemate, with little military action or diplomatic progress, even as tankers transiting Hormuz have come under Iranian attack. Qatar, which has mediated the talks, has said little publicly about their status. Iranian hardliners have taken last week’s US midterm results, which reflected the war’s unpopularity with American voters, as a sign that Washington may be more willing to accept Tehran’s demands on its nuclear programme and control of the strait.

At the same time, Washington appears to be adding pressure rather than easing it. The US military is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear programme. It has also set up a task force to stop Tehran moving advanced weapons and materials over land. Iran continues to struggle to sell crude under US sanctions, with billions of dollars in overseas assets frozen.

Diplomatic contacts have picked up since the midterms. Qatar said on Friday that Trump had called Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss de-escalation. That came a day after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke with counterparts across the Gulf and the wider region.

The next test is whether that flurry of calls turns into visible movement at the negotiating table, or whether the stalemate in Hormuz drags on. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Three risks for Nvidia shares after Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy
item.description:
Monday’s US session is the first chance for Nvidia shares to trade on the admission and the board inquiry, and the short-term risk leans lower. Three pressure points stand out. The first is key-person and governance risk at a founder-led company while an investigation is open. The second is Washington scrutiny that could cloud Huang’s role in shaping chip policy. The third is the China export question, if officials decide his influence on access to Beijing has been compromised. Nvidia’s heavy index weighting means a sharp move would weigh on the Nasdaq, the S&P 500 and AI-linked chip names. Offsetting that, leadership is unchanged and nothing so far touches demand, supply or earnings, so the selling could fade unless the story escalates.

---

Huang’s admission turns a disputed intelligence story into a confirmed personal one. That leaves Nvidia’s board, Congress and investors weighing whether the fallout stays reputational or starts to touch leadership and China policy.

Summary:

  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, apologising to his family and staff and taking full responsibility.
  • The relationship was with Alice Huang (Huang Le), a senior executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom US officials reportedly believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence.
  • Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation led by independent directors and outside counsel, and says it has no reason to believe secrets or national security were compromised.
  • Huang remains CEO and will cooperate. Nvidia had earlier described the contacts as routine customer dealings.
  • House committee chairs have requested a briefing, while Beijing calls the spying claims groundless.
  • Nvidia shares fell around 3% after the first report in late October. Monday’s session is the first test since the admission.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital relationship with a business executive whom US officials reportedly believe was working for Chinese intelligence. It sets up a test for shares of the world’s most valuable company when US trading resumes on Monday.

In a draft email to staff obtained by Axios, Huang apologised to his family and to employees, writing “I was unfaithful to my wife.” He said he took full responsibility for falling short of his duties to the company, its board and its shareholders.

The woman at the centre of the story is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company and Nvidia customer. She is not related to the Nvidia chief. Earlier reporting, citing US officials, said American intelligence had identified her as an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. According to those reports, she was tasked with gathering information from Huang and pushing for wider Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips. Beijing has rejected the allegations as groundless, and none of the reporting has shown that Huang knowingly passed on sensitive information.

Nvidia’s board responded on Sunday by opening an independent investigation, overseen by a committee of independent directors with outside counsel. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised, but that the inquiry would examine all available information. Huang will remain chief executive and has agreed to cooperate.

The admission marks a sharp shift from the company’s earlier stance. Since the first report surfaced in late October, Nvidia had described the contacts as routine dealings with a regional customer, noting that its chief executive meets thousands of customer executives each year. The shares fell around 3% on the day after that first report.

Pressure is also building in Washington. Republican chairs of House committees covering China, foreign affairs and intelligence have asked Huang for a briefing on the relationship and on Nvidia’s safeguards against espionage. President Donald Trump, who has relied on Huang as an adviser on artificial intelligence, has left open whether that role will continue.

For investors, the near-term question is whether this stays a governance and headline story or develops into something that touches Nvidia’s leadership or its access to China. The next markers to watch are further reporting on what information, if any, changed hands, the findings of the board’s inquiry and any congressional briefing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: WTI oil price outlook: After a 17.5% slide, can buyers reclaim $92.53?
item.description:
Oil recovered from a sharp selloff, but buyers have struggled to hold higher prices. My analysis finds a bearish picture over the next several sessions, while the immediate outlook is much less decisive. Here are the levels and developments that could change the outlook. Let's jump into my crude oil futures analysis on the daily chart:

WTI crude oil futures are attempting to stabilize after a roughly 17.5% decline from their late-October high, but the rebound has not yet overturned the recent bearish trend. December futures settled Friday, November 6, at $90.83 per barrel. The next meaningful test for buyers lies between $91 and $92.53.

The interesting part is not simply that oil has fallen and bounced. It is that selling pressure appears to be losing some of its effectiveness, but buyers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain a recovery.

That distinction could become particularly important as traders assess the next developments in the US-Iran conflict and their implications for global oil supply.

Oil's rebound has a problem: Buyers cannot hold their gains

WTI crude futures fell from approximately $104.99 in late October to $86.65 on November 5, a decline of about 17.5%.

From there, buyers managed to push prices back to $92.53 during Friday's session. But the recovery lost momentum, with our final market observation at $90.37 at 4:55 p.m. Eastern on November 6. That observation is separate from the day's official settlement of $90.83.

There is a potentially encouraging development for oil bulls. Recent attempts to push prices lower have not always produced lasting declines. That suggests the earlier selling pressure may be becoming less effective.

However, the opposite is also true. Buying interest has not consistently translated into sustained advances.

A market can stop falling rapidly without immediately becoming bullish.

The difference between a bounce and a genuine recovery is whether buyers can establish and defend higher prices.

Two market scores, two different conclusions

Our assessment of WTI crude futures, based on market evidence through November 6, produces two distinct readings:

Bigger picture: -6 out of 10 (bearish)

Over the recent weeks and looking toward the next several sessions, the market remains clearly tilted toward sellers. The rebound has not repaired the damage caused by the preceding decline.

Short term: -1 out of 10 (nearly balanced)

For the next one or two trading sessions, the evidence is considerably less directional. Buyers and sellers have both shown an ability to interrupt the other's progress.

The scoring scale runs from -10, representing exceptionally strong bearish pressure, to +10, representing exceptionally strong bullish pressure, with zero indicating a balanced market. These scores are directional assessments, not probabilities or automatic trading signals.

Remeber, oil traders: A market can remain bearish overall while offering a meaningful short-term recovery. The challenge is determining whether that recovery is developing into something more substantial.

WTI crude oil: Three scenarios worth watching

The next sustained move around $90-$92.53 could provide important information about the direction of oil prices.

1. Bullish scenario: A recovery above $92.53 changes the picture

The first encouraging development would be a move above $91.00-$91.32, followed by evidence that prices can remain above this area.

That would indicate that the recovery is gaining some traction.

The more significant test comes at $92.53, Friday's session high.

A sustained break above that level, particularly if oil can successfully hold it on a subsequent pullback, would strengthen the argument that buyers are regaining control.

If this happens, the next historical price references to monitor are:

  • $93.59: The first higher area where the recovery could face another test.

  • $95.15: A further upside reference if buying continues.

These are potential reaction levels, not predictions that oil will necessarily reach them.

A failed recovery that sends prices back below $90 would weaken this bullish scenario.

2. Bearish scenario: Failure around $91 puts $89.07 back in focus

The bearish scenario becomes more convincing if oil cannot recover $91 and instead falls back below $90.00-$90.05, remaining beneath that area.

That would suggest buyers are still unable to maintain higher prices.

The next important level would be $89.07, Friday's trading-session low.

A sustained break beneath $89.07 would increase the possibility of another decline toward the lower historical support area at $87.13-$86.65.

This would reinforce the broader bearish assessment.

Conversely, recovering and holding above the broken levels would weaken the bearish interpretation.

3. Neutral scenario: Oil remains trapped around $90-$91

Not every market needs to produce an immediate directional opportunity.

WTI could continue moving back and forth around $90-$91 without establishing a sustained breakout.

That would be consistent with the nearly balanced short-term score.

In such conditions, isolated moves above resistance or below support can produce misleading signals. Waiting for evidence that prices can hold beyond an important level may provide a clearer picture than reacting to every price fluctuation.

Why geopolitics could overwhelm the technical picture

There is an important fundamental dimension to this oil price outlook.

Much of the recent volatility has been associated with shifting expectations about the US-Iran conflict and the prospects for restoring more reliable oil shipments from the Middle East.

As investingLive recently explained, the possibility of de-escalation has created downward pressure on oil prices, while renewed military action remains a risk.

Reports of tanker attacks have also revived concerns about regional supply disruptions.

This creates two quite different potential drivers of oil prices:

De-escalation and improved supply conditions: Reduced fears of disruption could remove some of the geopolitical risk premium embedded in oil prices, potentially reinforcing the recent decline.

Renewed conflict or shipping disruptions: An increase in perceived supply risks could support oil prices or produce another sharp recovery, even if the recent technical trend remains bearish.

There are also conventional supply-and-demand considerations.

On November 1, seven OPEC+ producers announced that they would maintain their required production levels for December at September's levels.

Meanwhile, the latest US Energy Information Administration inventory report, released November 4, showed US commercial crude inventories declining by approximately 0.9 million barrels in the week ending October 30.

The inventory decline is a reminder that a sharp oil selloff does not necessarily mean every indicator of physical supply and demand is weakening.

For the coming week, the next scheduled EIA petroleum inventory release is Thursday, November 12, at noon Eastern, delayed because of the Veterans Day holiday.

What falling oil prices might mean for stocks, inflation and currencies

Even investors who never trade crude oil directly may find the next move informative.

Oil prices influence several important parts of the global economy, but their meaning depends heavily on why prices are changing.

Consider two very different reasons for lower oil prices.

If oil declines because supply disruptions are easing, that could help reduce energy-related inflation pressure and eventually benefit fuel-intensive businesses.

But if oil declines because economic demand is deteriorating, the same price movement could signal a less encouraging outlook for economic activity and corporate earnings.

There is another distinction worth remembering: Lower crude prices do not automatically translate into equally large declines in gasoline or diesel prices.

Refining capacity, fuel inventories and the margins earned by refineries can influence what consumers and businesses actually pay. This is an important theme in investingLive's recent analysis of oil refining margins and the prospects for normalizing fuel prices.

For energy-company investors, lower crude prices may pressure producers' revenues and margins, while companies that consume significant amounts of fuel could benefit. The outcome also depends on each company's cost structure, hedging and broader economic conditions.

For currency traders, changes in oil prices can influence the economic outlook for oil-exporting and oil-importing countries, although exchange rates respond to many other forces as well.

Oil should therefore be treated as a supporting market signal, not a stand-alone forecast for inflation, stocks, bonds or currencies.

What would convince us that oil's outlook is changing?

For now, the evidence supports a relatively straightforward conclusion.

WTI's recent-weeks trend remains bearish, but there are signs that the preceding selloff is losing some of its force. The immediate outlook is more balanced, and neither buyers nor sellers have decisively established control.

A sustained recovery above $91.00-$91.32, followed by a convincing move above $92.53, would strengthen the case for higher oil prices.

Conversely, renewed weakness below $90, followed by a sustained break of $89.07, would increase the risk of another move toward $87.13-$86.65.

And if oil continues fluctuating between these areas, the most useful conclusion may simply be that the market has not yet made its next directional decision.

The analysis refers specifically to NYMEX December 2026 WTI crude futures, with market evidence through November 6, 2026. The levels are historical references, not live prices or guaranteed support and resistance. Other futures expiries and oil instruments may trade at different prices.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold analysis: Buyers keep defending $4,040. Is $4,140 the next target?
item.description:
Gold futures buyers keep returning near $4,040. Is $4,140 the next test?

Gold's recovery looks more convincing than Friday's volatile price action suggests. Buyers have repeatedly defended an important support area, and underlying trading activity points to improving buying effectiveness. But one resistance zone still stands between gold and a potentially larger rebound.

Gold futures are showing signs that buyers may be gaining the upper hand after a volatile week. The recovery from Friday's low of $4,035.10 is encouraging, but my bullish interpretation goes beyond that single rebound. Several developments suggest that gold may be preparing for another attempt toward $4,135-$4,140, provided buyers can overcome nearby resistance.

Why I see more bullish signs than bearish ones in gold

One price area stands out in my analysis: $4,040-$4,050.

Around $4,040 sits the October 29 point of control (POC), the price at which the greatest amount of trading volume occurred during that session.

That makes it a useful reference for understanding where buyers and sellers previously conducted significant business.

Gold moved above this level on November 4, retested the area and subsequently continued its advance.

The rally eventually carried futures beyond $4,150 on November 5.

What happened next is particularly interesting.

The market retraced sharply, and on Friday, November 6, gold returned to approximately $4,035, briefly moving beneath that important $4,040 reference.

Once again, buyers responded.

Gold recovered toward $4,080, reclaiming both the $4,040 area and the psychologically important $4,050 level.

To me, the repeated response around this price region is a meaningful bullish development. It suggests buyers have been willing to defend an area that previously attracted considerable trading activity.

Of course, support can eventually fail. But until it does, repeated rebounds deserve attention.

What the underlying trading activity tells us

Our deeper examination of Friday's trading adds another dimension to this interpretation.

The initial recovery attempt was unsuccessful. Sellers returned, and the market struggled to establish upward momentum.

Later, however, conditions improved.

Selling pressure became less effective at producing additional downside progress. Buyers established a higher low and subsequently achieved a stronger recovery.

Trading activity also became concentrated at higher prices during the rebound, suggesting improving buyer participation.

This is the part of the analysis I find especially constructive.

It is one thing for gold to bounce because selling temporarily stops. It is another for buyers to begin achieving progressively better price results.

Friday's developments showed elements of the latter.

Nevertheless, this remains an early indication rather than proof that sellers have lost control. Gold still needs to demonstrate that it can sustain trading above nearby resistance.

Three technical reasons the recovery may have further to run

Beyond Friday's buying activity, the broader price structure provides additional support for the bullish argument.

1. The recovery developed from a substantial base

Gold reached $3,879.30 on October 30 before stabilizing over the following sessions.

From October 30 into the beginning of November 4, the market established a foundation for a potential reversal.

The subsequent advance toward $4,155.80 represented a recovery of more than $275 per ounce from that October low.

That is a meaningful move, not merely a minor intraday bounce.

The correction that followed has been substantial, but it has not erased the entire advance.

2. Multiple technical references converge near $4,040

In addition to October 29's point of control, an October 27 volume-weighted average price (VWAP) reference sits near $4,038.

VWAP measures the average trading price weighted by volume. Historical VWAP references can sometimes become important areas where the market reassesses previous trading activity.

The proximity of these references to Friday's $4,035.10 low creates an interesting support cluster.

That does not make the cluster unbreakable, but it provides a reason to pay close attention to how gold behaves when returning to this area.

3. Friday's recovery reclaimed another important reference

Friday's VWAP was approximately $4,069.

The latest chart snapshot shows gold finishing near $4,080, above that reference and above the $4,050 support region.

For me, that is another encouraging observation.

After a significant intraday decline, recovering above the session's volume-weighted average suggests that buyers were capable of regaining meaningful ground.

The market did not simply stop falling. It recovered into a more constructive position.

The bigger picture: Three timeframes are beginning to support the recovery

The daily chart shows an emerging reversal attempt following October's substantial correction.

The four-hour chart shows the first meaningful pullback following the advance toward $4,155.80.

The hourly chart, meanwhile, shows early stabilization and improving short-term momentum.

These developments can coexist without contradiction.

A daily bullish recovery can experience a four-hour correction while the hourly chart begins signaling renewed buying interest.

The important question is whether the shorter-term recovery can develop into another advance on the higher timeframes.

For now, the technical evidence is encouraging but not fully aligned.

What could take gold toward $4,135-$4,140?

Although my interpretation leans bullish, the market still faces an important obstacle.

The immediate resistance area is $4,084-$4,092.

Gold needs to establish sustained trading above this region to strengthen the case that buyers are taking control.

A convincing break would bring $4,098-$4,116 into focus.

Beyond that, I would be watching $4,123-$4,135 and particularly the $4,135-$4,140 resistance area, which I consider a plausible next destination for the recovery.

That would place gold within striking distance of its previous $4,155.80 recovery high.

My view is not that gold must travel to $4,140.

Rather, the repeated defense of lower prices, improving underlying buying activity and broader recovery structure make that an increasingly interesting possibility.

A failure to overcome $4,092 would delay this scenario and could lead to another test of support.

Gold futures tradeCompass: Levels for Monday, November 9

The following conditional tradeCompass map applies to COMEX December 2026 gold futures, based on the November 6 analysis.

Bullish scenario: Above $4,092

Sustained trading above $4,092 would strengthen the recovery outlook.

  • First partial-profit target: $4,104

  • Second partial-profit target: $4,130

  • Third partial-profit target: $4,149

The $4,135-$4,140 resistance region remains an important area to assess between the second and third targets.

A successful retest of former resistance would provide more convincing evidence than a brief move above the threshold.

Bearish scenario: Below $4,050

A sustained decline beneath $4,050 would weaken the immediate bullish case.

  • First partial-profit target: $4,039

  • Second partial-profit target: $4,007

  • Third partial-profit target: $3,992

The $4,038-$4,040 cluster could still attract buying interest, so a break below $4,050 alone would not prove that the entire recovery has failed.

A further decline below Friday's $4,035.10 low would be more significant, raising the risk of a deeper correction.

Neutral scenario: Between $4,050 and $4,092

Gold remains within a decision area until either side demonstrates more convincing control.

Traders may prefer to monitor price behavior near the boundaries rather than chase a move in the middle.

Partial-profit taking and reducing remaining risk after the first target are possible management considerations. Any stop placement and position size should be determined by the actual instrument, the technical invalidation and the trader's risk tolerance.

For a fuller explanation, see how traders can use investingLive's tradeCompass.

My outlook for gold: Bullish, but confirmation still matters

Having examined the underlying trading activity alongside the broader technical structure, I currently see more encouraging bullish signs than bearish ones.

The recovery from the October 30 low was substantial. Friday's pullback returned to an important support cluster, and buyers responded with renewed strength.

Perhaps most importantly, selling pressure appears to be losing some of its effectiveness.

That leads me to favor the possibility of another recovery attempt, potentially toward $4,135-$4,140.

But there is a difference between having a bullish interpretation and knowing what the market will do next.

If gold cannot overcome $4,092, my expectation needs to be reassessed. If the market subsequently loses $4,050 and breaks below $4,035, the immediate bullish argument becomes substantially weaker.

For now, the evidence suggests buyers are fighting back effectively. The next test is whether they can turn that improvement into sustained progress above resistance.

item.title: Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles to be replaced by Stephen Miller
item.description:
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles will be leaving her post, President Trump reported. She will move over to the Trump political operation, he said. 

Her replacement is Stephen Miller, who Trump said is "one of my most trusted advisors". Miller was the deputy chief of staff.

Bloomberg reports that Wiles resigned on Thursday night, so this impetus could have come from her, rather than Trump.

In any case, Miller is an extreme hawk on immigration and that's what he is best known for. He becamse less prominent after the immigration roundups in Minnesota. Perhaps more importantly, Miller has been one of the most forceful public defenders of Trump's 2026 war against Iran.

This could be an early signal that Trump has no plans to make peace or to dial down tariffs. Instead, he may escalate on both fronts in order to re-cast his legacy as someone who made tough choices for the long term. 

In April, Miller argued that the American blockade could continue indefinitely if Iran refused a deal. He also threatened the potential destruction of Iranian energy infrastructure, although he described that as a last resort.

Behind closed doors, there hasn't been much reporting on his stance, so he might just be touting the usual White House talking points. In any case, moving Miller  from deputy chief of staff to the top staff position increases his potential influence over which recommendations reach Trump and how decisions are implemented. In almost all aspects, he is more ideological that Wiles.

Update: There is a report from Maggie Haberman, who is highly credible, and wrote:

"Miller’s pitch for the job, according to people who heard it, was that the president needed to wind down the Iran war, a conflict that the president’s core supporters viewed as a betrayal."

That's a good sign towards a reopening of Hormuz.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Daly: Jobs report is good news
item.description:
The Fed’s Daly spoke on CNBC about the jobs report, wages and inflation.

  • Job report good news

  • Wage growth isn’t booming

  • Real wages are falling

  • Feel hopeful when think about American workforce

  • On inflation, would like confidence to be higher

  • High inflation for too long

  • inflation has to be number 1 priority.

  • Strong labor market gives Fed latitude to get job done on inflation. Rate hike was right move, also good to be on hold at last meeting.

  • Uncertainty and tariffs, war, AI, but inflation is more stubborn than would like.

  • Will have to tighten policy further.

  • Prepared to raise rates if it is called for

  • Thinks the Fed needs to be deliberate

  • How much more tightening and when need more information

  • The AI trade has to be orderly.

  • Quite a bit commitment to AI.  

  • If they are repressing signals slowing of demand, might see growth come down a little.

  • Not worried about substantial decline in growth

  • Businesses want inflation to come down.

  • Businesses are cautiously optimistic about outlook.

  • Full employment looks to be pretty stable. 

  • When he stepped back from painful volatility, this is a kind of rebalancing that you would hope for.

Analysis

Daly’s message was hawkish. Inflation is her number one priority, and a resilient labor market gives the Fed room to bring it down. She welcomed the jobs report and sees full employment as broadly stable, but she also pointed out that wage growth isn’t booming and real wages are falling. That distinction matters. The jobs market can hold up while inflation still eats into workers’ purchasing power.

On rates, Daly said the hike was the right move and that holding at the last meeting also made sense. She expects further tightening and is prepared to raise rates if warranted, but she wants more information before deciding when to move and how far to go. For traders, the jobs report gives the Fed latitude. The inflation data will help determine when it uses it.

On AI, Daly sees substantial investment commitments and wants the adjustment in the trade to be orderly. If the volatility is signaling softer demand, she sees room for growth to slow a little. Her broader read is that businesses remain cautiously optimistic, employment looks stable, and the economy is going through the kind of rebalancing she would hope to see. That leaves stubborn inflation as the more pressing concern for policy.

Daly is a voting member in 2027.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US presses China to honor Busan trade truce as rare earth shipments fall short.
item.description:
The US is pressing China to immediately fulfill the commitments Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping made in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer raised concerns with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and stressed that further progress depends on concrete results.

Rare earths are the sticking point. US officials told the Financial Times that China has fulfilled only about two-thirds of its commitments and has failed to increase supply as Washington expected. Beijing disputes the US assessment. One material in focus is yttrium, used in jet engines and missiles. The FT reports that Chinese export restrictions are affecting Japanese suppliers that serve US manufacturers.

What did the two sides agree to in Busan?

  • Rare earths and critical minerals. China agreed to suspend the broader export controls it announced in October 2025 and issue general export licenses for rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite for US end users and their suppliers worldwide.

  • Agriculture. China agreed to buy at least 12 million metric tons of US soybeans in the final two months of 2025 and at least 25 million metric tons annually from 2026 through 2028. It also agreed to resume purchases of US sorghum and lumber and suspend a range of retaliatory tariffs. The FT reports that US officials say China is meeting its soybean pledge but falling short on some other agricultural purchases.

  • Tariffs and other measures. Under the original deal, the US agreed to keep higher reciprocal tariffs on hold, cut fentanyl-related tariffs by 10 percentage points and pause certain export-control and shipping measures. China agreed to tighten controls on chemicals used to make fentanyl and ease some measures affecting US semiconductor companies.

What should traders watch now?

The truce has been extended through January 10, 2027, according to the FT. The near-term barometer is whether export approvals translate into more material reaching US manufacturers and their suppliers. If shipments pick up, that gives both sides something concrete to point to heading into the next round of talks. If supply stays tight, rare earths could become a bigger obstacle to another extension as the January deadline approaches.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin testing a key support target. What needs to happen to give buyers some relief?
item.description:
Bitcoin moved higher with stocks in the risk-on trade that followed the election results. Yesterday, that trade went into reverse. As AI concerns sent stocks tumbling, Bitcoin gave up its post-election gains, fell back below its 100-day moving average and returned to a swing area that has repeatedly come into play since August.

In the video above, I walk through the chart and outline what needs to happen to give buyers some relief. Where can buyers lean with close risk? What levels would they need to get above to take back some control? And where does the price have room to roam if the floor gives way?

The swing area is the immediate barometer.

Bitcoin was trading near $75,632 at the time of the chart, inside the swing area between $74,925 and $76,052. The upper end is the 38.2% retracement of the move up from the July low. The lower end is the floor buyers need to defend.

As long as the price holds above $74,925, buyers have a level to lean against with close risk. The first sign of relief would be a move back above $76,052 that can hold. That would take the price out of the swing area and give buyers a shot at the next upside target.

The moving averages are the next hurdles.

The 100-day moving average comes in at $77,061. Get above that and stay above, and traders can start to eye the 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages at $77,631 and $77,795, respectively. Those two hourly averages are close enough to treat as a zone. A move through both would give buyers more confidence and open the door to the next swing level near $79,146.

Until the price starts reclaiming those levels, sellers still have the technical edge.

A break of the floor would give sellers more room.

Move below $74,925 and stay below, and the focus shifts to the 200-day moving average at $73,190. Below that, the next target is the 50% midpoint of the move up from the July low at $72,554.

The distinction I’m watching is what happens after a break. A dip below $74,925 that quickly moves back into the swing area would put sellers on alert for a failed break. A break that stays below the floor, especially if a bounce stalls back near $74,925, would show that sellers are starting to lean against the old support. That’s the price action that would put the lower targets in play.

item.title: November US UMich prelim consumer sentiment 51.0 vs 48.0 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 46.3
  • Current conditions 51.0 vs 48.0 expected
  • Expectations 50.9 vs 49.5 expected
  • One-year inflation 4.3 vs 4.7% prior
  • Five-year inflation 3.4 vs 3.5% prior

The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers is one of the oldest measures of US household sentiment but it's lost its lustre in financial markets due to readings that don't correspond with spending. The preliminary reading is released at 10 am ET in the first half of each month, based on interviews conducted over the preceding weeks. A final reading incorporating the full sample follows near the end of the month. The preliminary figure sometimes draws a market reaction because it’s the first look at the month.

The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment is built from questions about personal finances, business conditions and whether it’s a good time to buy big-ticket items. It’s indexed to 100 in early 1966. The survey splits into two sub-indexes, current economic conditions and consumer expectations. The expectations measure is a component of the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index.

Inflation expectations are lately the most market-sensitive part of the release and the Fed will be pleased with the dip in today's report. Respondents estimate price changes over the next year and over the next five to 10 years. The Federal Reserve watches the longer-run measure as a signal of whether inflation expectations remain anchored, and sharp moves can shift Treasury yields and rate pricing. Because the preliminary sample is smaller, these figures can be revised meaningfully in the final release.

The survey moved from telephone to online interviews in 2024, complicating comparisons with its long history. Responses have also become increasingly partisan, with sentiment swinging sharply depending on which party controls the White House.

Sentiment readings don’t always match spending, and households often keep buying even when they say they’re pessimistic. Still, the survey provides a timely read on how consumers are reacting to inflation, tariffs, gasoline prices, the job market and stock prices. I'd argue they were a good indicator of what was coming in the midterms, rather than what is/was coming in the economy.

item.title: US October non-farm payrolls +165K vs +65K expected
item.description:
• Prior was +29K (revised to +60K)
  • Two-month net revision +84K
  • Unemployment rate 4.1% vs 4.2% expected
  • Prior unemployment rate 4.2%
  • Unrounded unemployment 4.141% vs 4.1753% prior
  • Participation rate 61.9% vs 61.8% prior
  • U6 underemployment rate 7.9% vs 7.6% prior
  • Average hourly earnings +0.4% m/m vs +0.3% expected
  • Average hourly earnings 3.1% y/y vs +2.9% expected
  • Average weekly hours 34.4 vs 34.4 expected
  • Change in private payrolls +159K vs +64K expected
  • Prior private payrolls +46K (revised to +78K)
  • Change in manufacturing payrolls 19K vs +5K expected
  • Government payrolls +6K vs -17K prior
  • Household survey +463K

This is a beat from bottom to top and the wage growth will certainly make the Fed look twice. They will get another jobs report before the December 9 FOMC but this one will certainly make it more likely that they will hike rates.

If there is a hint of weakness in the report is the rise in U6. Part-time for economic reasons rose +339k to 4.84M. Almost all of it came from “slack work or business conditions” (+356k). That’s employers cutting hours.

US 2-year yields are up 4.5 bps on the day to 4.52% and USD/JPY is up 72 pips to 158.38. S&P 500 futures are still slightly higher but I think the stock market is focused on things other than macro at the moment.

Note that last month was a soft one across the board so there isn't necessarily momentum here but there are no real signs of weakness, especially considering that most of the pre-NFP jobs data was also strong for October.

Another interesting point is that there is a bifurcation in the construction center between data centers and everything else. Nonresidential specialty trade contractors are +101k y/y. Residential specialty contractors are -36k y/y, including -15.2k in October alone. Higher rates won't help unwind that.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada Employment change for October -4.7K vs 13.6K estimate. Unemployment rate 6.7%.
item.description:
• Prior month -68.3K

Details:

  • Employment change −4,700 vs +13,600 expected. Prior −68,000.

  • Unemployment rate 6.7% vs 6.5% expected. Prior 6.5%.

  • Employment rate 60.5% vs 60.6% in September.

  • Average hourly wages +2.2% year over year vs +2.3% in September, before seasonal adjustment.

  • Full time employment -18.1K vs -35.4K last month

  • Part Time employment 13.4K v -32.9k last month 

October components compared with September

  • Youth unemployment 13.7% vs 13.0%.

  • Unemployment among people aged 55 and older 5.5% vs 5.3%.

  • Educational services employment +15,000 vs −35,000.

  • Alberta employment −24,000 vs +23,000.

  • British Columbia employment +12,000 vs −20,000.

Canada’s October jobs report came in weaker than expected on both headline measures. Statistics Canada reported that employment was little changed, down 4,700 after declines of 68,000 in September and 42,000 in August. The unemployment rate rose to 6.7% as 33,000 more people looked for work.

The private sector was the soft spot. Private-sector employment fell 53,000, its first decline since February, while public-sector employment rose 50,000. Wholesale and retail trade lost 29,000 jobs, while construction added 16,000 and educational services added 15,000.

Here is the graphic of where the jobs were gained and lossed:

Quick analysis

The private-sector decline and slower wage growth give the Bank of Canada a reason to be cautious about another hike after it raised its policy rate to 2.50% in October. The offset is energy-driven inflation. The Bank raised rates because it was concerned that higher energy costs would spread to other prices. On its own, the jobs miss would normally weigh on the Canadian dollar and short-term Canadian yields, putting upward pressure on USDCAD.

The USDCAD moves higher

The combination of the stronger US jobs report and the Canada weaker look, has pushed the USDCAD to a new high for the day and going back to October 20. The price has also moved above a swing area target between 1.4068 to 1.40828 (inclusive of the borken 38.2%).  The next target? 1.4110.  

What this report measures

Statistics Canada’s monthly Labour Force Survey estimates how many people are employed and what share of the labour force is unemployed. The headline employment and unemployment figures are seasonally adjusted to make month-to-month comparisons easier. Traders watch the report for signs of labour-market slack and wage pressure that could influence Bank of Canada policy.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart | Nasdaq futures rebound after rout as U.S. and Canadian jobs reports loom
item.description:
Life goes on after yesterday’s tumble in stocks. The Nasdaq 100 took the biggest hit, falling 6.36% for its worst day since March 2020. The selling went well beyond the tech-heavy index.

  • Dow −3.4%

  • S&P 500 −4.36%

  • Nasdaq Composite −5.52%

  • Nasdaq 100 −6.36%

There’s a bid in Nasdaq futures this morning, but the Dow is still under pressure and European shares are broadly lower. That makes the early bounce a mixed signal heading into the U.S. and Canadian jobs reports. The 10-year Treasury yield is also higher, near 4.86%. If payrolls surprise, I’ll watch whether yields and the dollar confirm the first move in stocks or whether that move fades. The tech selloff also carried into Asian trading. investingLive Asia-Pacific news wrap

The U.S. dollar is higher across the majors

The dollar has gained the most against the NZD (+0.82%) and AUD (+0.75%). It is also higher against the JPY (+0.40%), EUR (+0.39%), GBP (+0.37%), CAD (+0.30%) and CHF (+0.22%). The Swiss franc has held up best against the greenback.

The dollar is near the session highs against the yen and near the strongest levels of the morning against the euro and sterling. The first test after payrolls is whether those extremes break and hold. A quick reversal back into the range would tell me the first move failed to attract follow-through. In the video above, I take a technical look and outline the levels for the EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD given the run higher in the US dollar today.

Currency ranges ahead of the data

Using the quoted session highs and lows and the 22-day average ranges (about a months trading range), the major currency pairs have for the most part met and exceeded their averages underscoring the volatility and movement today.

  • EURUSD 1.1168–1.1234, 66 pips or 105% of average.

  • USDJPY 157.26–158.37, 111 pips or 129% of average.

  • GBPUSD 1.3382–1.3463, 81 pips or 116% of average.

  • USDCHF 0.8148–0.8189, 41 pips or 77% of average.

  • USDCAD 1.4009–1.4081, 72 pips or 111% of average.

  • AUDUSD 0.6863–0.6942, 79 pips or 161% of average.

  • NZDUSD 0.5541–0.5606, 65 pips or 141% of average.

USDCHF has the most room relative to its normal range. AUDUSD and NZDUSD has already stretched the furthest with risk-off sentiment and prospects for lower growth hurting those pairs. USDCAD is also past its average before either jobs report has landed. With both reports due at the same time, the bigger move in USDCAD would come if the surprises pull the two currencies in opposite directions. Stronger U.S. data and weaker Canadian data would favor the upside, while the reverse would favor the downside.

Stocks, yields and commodities

At 8:00 a.m. ET, U.S. futures were implying a split open in volatile trading.

  • Dow −570 points

  • S&P 500 +11 points

  • Nasdaq 100 +359 points

The selling continued across Europe, with Germany and the UK both down more than 2%.

  • German DAX −2.21%

  • UK FTSE 100 −2.05%

  • French CAC 40 −1.63%

  • Spanish IBEX 35 −1.27%

  • Italian FTSE MIB −1.06%

U.S. Treasury yields are higher across the curve. Yields are down from the 5.36% high reached a few weeks ago in the 10 year but the bounce back higher today is showing some constraint on the downside..

  • 2-year 4.491%, up 1.37 basis points

  • 5-year 4.629%, up 2.09 basis points

  • 10-year 4.864%, up 2.65 basis points

  • 30-year 5.284%, up 3.26 basis points

WTI crude is up $0.47 at $90.99 after trading between $89.07 and $92.53. Spot gold is down about 0.5% near $4,068, while silver is up 0.58% near $52.07. Copper is little changed near $6.27, and Bitcoin is nearly flat at $76,031.

North American calendar

  • 8:30 a.m. ET — U.S. October jobs report. Nonfarm payrolls are expected to rise 65K after 29K, with private payrolls expected at +64K after +46K and manufacturing payrolls at +5K after +9K. Unemployment is expected to hold at 4.2%. Average hourly earnings are forecast to rise 0.3% on the month after 0.1%, with annual growth easing to 2.9% from 3.0%. The average workweek is expected to hold at 34.4 hours.

  • 8:30 a.m. ET — Canada October jobs report. Employment is expected to rise 13.6K after a 68.3K decline, with unemployment forecast to hold at 6.5%. Last month’s losses were split between full-time jobs (−35.4K) and part-time jobs (−32.9K). I’ll watch whether full-time employment participates in any rebound.

  • 10:00 a.m. ET — University of Michigan preliminary November sentiment. The headline index is expected at 48.0, unchanged from October’s final reading. Current conditions are expected at 48.0 versus 46.7, and expectations at 49.5 versus 48.8.

For the U.S. report, I’ll look at revisions and wages alongside the payroll headline. A payroll beat accompanied by softer wages could get a different reaction in yields than a beat with hotter earnings. That distinction matters for the dollar and for a Nasdaq trying to recover from yesterday’s selloff.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

EURUSD — Sellers have the edge near the session low

EURUSD is at 1.1174, just six pips above the 1.1168 low. That low is the first downside target. A break that holds below it would give sellers more control. If the break fails, 1.1200 is the first upside barometer. A move back above that round number would put the prior close at 1.1218 in play, followed by the session high at 1.1234.

USDJPY — Buyers are pressing 158.37

USDJPY is at 158.29, eight pips below the session high at 158.37. The buyers have the stronger hand above 158.00, which gives them a nearby level to lean against. A break and hold above 158.37 would extend the move and put 158.50 in focus. Back below 158.00, the bias softens and the prior close at 157.66 becomes the next downside reference, followed by 157.26.

GBPUSD — The 1.3400 area is the first barometer

GBPUSD is at 1.3399. Staying below 1.3400 keeps the focus on the 1.3382 session low. A sustained break there would give sellers more control. If buyers reclaim and hold above 1.3400, the next upside references are the prior close at 1.3449 and the session high at 1.3463.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
